Antibiotic PK/PD modeling starts with one awkward fact: bacteria do not “see” the dose. They see **concentration over time** at the effect site, relative to a susceptibility threshold — usually the **MIC**.

This lesson is for modelers and microbiologists who want the indices to stop feeling like slogans.

::: {.callout-note}
## Scope
Educational modeling intuition — not a dosing guide and not a substitute for clinical guidelines.
:::

## The MIC is a threshold, not a full phenotype

The **minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC)** is the lowest concentration that prevents visible growth under a defined assay. It is useful because it compresses susceptibility into a number we can put next to an exposure curve.

It is also incomplete:

- Assay conditions can move the measured floor.
- Tolerance and persistence can leave survivors even when the MIC looks favorable.
- Protein binding means free (unbound) exposure often matters more than total concentration.

For simulation, treat MIC as a **scenario input with uncertainty**, not as biological truth.

## Three classic indices

Most antibacterial PK/PD targets fall into one of three families:

| Index | Rough idea | Typical drug classes |
|-------|------------|----------------------|
| **fT>MIC** | Fraction of the dosing interval that free concentration stays above MIC | Many β-lactams |
| **fAUC/MIC** | Integrated free exposure scaled by MIC | Fluoroquinolones, vancomycin (often) |
| **fCmax/MIC** | Peak free concentration relative to MIC | Some concentration-dependent agents |

The leading **f** means unbound fraction. If you simulate total concentrations but apply a free-drug target, you are mixing units.

## How to choose an index in a model

Ask three questions before coding a target:

1. **Is killing time-dependent or concentration-dependent** for this class in the literature you trust?
2. **Are you modeling free or total drug?** Align the PK output with the PD target.
3. **Is the target joint?** Combinations (for example β-lactam + inhibitor) may need two simultaneous conditions.

If the literature reports a target as “100% fT>MIC” or “fAUC/MIC ≥ 125,” that is a **decision rule for simulation**, not proof that every patient at that threshold is cured.

## Takeaway for modelers

- Put **units and binding** next to every target.
- Sample MIC from a distribution when you care about population performance.
- Keep the index choice **traceable to a cited source**, the same way you would cite a clearance equation.
